Dentin hypersensitivity

Clinical studies often report reduced sensitivity, while some controlled comparisons are null or do not show a clear advantage over active treatments. Protocols and outcome timing vary.

PBM Database summary

What the records report

Clinical studies often report reduced sensitivity, while some controlled comparisons are null or do not show a clear advantage over active treatments. Protocols and outcome timing vary.

Summary of the Evidence

The database lists 52 records under “Dentin hypersensitivity”: 44 human clinical reports/trials, four meta-analyses, one systematic review, one protocol, one rat experiment and one in-vitro study. The reviews synthesize overlapping trials, not independent cohorts; laser classes and adjuncts vary. One indexed 2025 report concerns post-scaling/root-planing sensitivity, making it indirect evidence.

Human and clinical evidence

Many small trials report reduced sensitivity, but results range from positive to no between-group benefit. A double-blind trial found no difference from control, while other randomized studies report benefit at follow-up; protocols and co-interventions differ substantially (Ko et al., 2014; Shan et al., 2023; Barbosa et al., 2026). Many studies assess immediate sensitivity after a stimulus, so response timing and stimulus type matter. Short-term symptom change should not be equated with durable tubule occlusion or modification of the underlying cause. The mixed results and varied adjuncts support caution when comparing individual protocols.

Primary original study: Ishikiriama et al. 2025 review of 20 randomized trials:, PubMed

Animal evidence

One rat model found 660- and 808-nm PBM reversed experimentally induced thermal hypersensitivity (de Oliveira et al., 2021).

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

One cell study combined bioactive glass with laser phototherapy and measured stem-cell proliferation and differentiation (Lopez et al., 2017).

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

The 2025 randomized report used a 980 nm near-infrared diode laser at 0.8 W, 10 Hz, for 30 seconds, with a reported energy density of 99.17 J/cm², alone or over fluoride varnish. Sensitivity was measured immediately and at 7, 30, and 180 days. The review includes different laser classes and doses, so this specific protocol is not a pooled treatment setting.

Interpretation

Pain after a stimulus is not the same outcome as durable tubule sealing or correction of the underlying cause. Short-term changes should be interpreted with the stimulus and follow-up in view. Heterogeneous protocols and active comparators limit the conclusion that one PBM schedule works across all patients.

Evidence strength in source summaryLow. Many studies report less sensitivity, but protocols and controlled results vary.
Publications and records52 unique titles.

Evidence strength rationale and next steps

The evidence includes randomized trials, other clinical reports, case reports, animal and in-vitro experiments, and reviews that reuse overlapping trials. Many studies report reduced sensitivity, but comparators, laser types, stimuli, co-interventions, and follow-up differ. Recent randomized evidence also compares laser with fluoride varnish rather than establishing one common treatment effect.
